doc.title: Phoebe Jacobs and Jackie Harris interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 21, 2006

title: Armstrong's collages, scissors and reading
summary: Jacobs describes his tape collages, ceiling collage and curiosity, including his reading about Hitler.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: We’re lucky that he was so into writing letters and recording things. When I visited the Archive and Michael —
The tape boxes that he would—
When did he have time to do that if he was working, in between shows?

You know one of the things that I had to dispose of in the house must have been 14 pairs of scissors, you know little scissors that you’d cut paper dolls stuff. ‘Cause wherever Louis went he’d get a new pair of scissors or his scissors wasn’t sharp enough or something. So he’d come home with two scissors. And Lucille would have a drawer with all the scissors that he had. But he loved, in fact one time he said to her this room is mine, right, the den? He did the collage all over the ceiling. When I came in there I couldn’t believe it. I said, “You’ve got to be kidding, what do people have to lay down and look up at your ceiling?”

But you know his collages were so revealing. One of his collages he has a huge picture of himself and in that picture of himself he’s got pictures of Malcolm X, Duke Ellington, all in his brain, all the men that he admired. Did you ever see that collage?

Dynamite. I mean Louis was so intelligent. He was so well read. You know when I saw a book on Hitler on Louis’s shelf I said to him, “Pops, how the hell do you read about this monster?” He said, “Look, you’ve got to know why you’re hating somebody.” He just felt if they’re going to put it in a library and people are going to talk about it you have to learn it. You have to learn all this. And he had it. That’s the last present I gave him was a book on birds and foliage because Lucille fixed the garden and she wanted him to recuperate out in the garden and he loved to learn about plants and different things that she had back there. He was very curious about life around him. He was an amazing human being. There’ll never be another Louis. © Fillius Jazz Archive -19-
